home.description: Everyone goes through changes as they grow up. This app helps you understand these changes in a friendly, easy-to-understand way.

boys.title: For Boys
boys.subtitle: Understanding Menstruation
boys.intro: Learning about menstruation helps you understand and support the people in your life.
boys.whyLearnContent: Understanding menstruation helps you be a better friend, brother, and family member. It breaks down barriers and helps everyone feel more comfortable.
boys.whatIsContent: Menstruation, or having a period, is a natural monthly process that happens in the female body. It's a sign that the body is healthy and working normally.
boys.howToHelpContent: Be understanding, don't make jokes about periods, and be supportive if someone needs help or feels unwell.

basics.title: Understanding Menstruation: The Basics
basics.intro: Let's start with the simple facts about menstruation. It's a natural process that happens in healthy bodies.
basics.whatIsText: Menstruation (also called a period) is when blood and tissue from the uterus comes out through the vagina. This happens once a month for most people with female reproductive systems.
basics.whyHappensText: Every month, the body prepares for a possible pregnancy. The uterus creates a soft, cushiony lining. If pregnancy doesn't happen, this lining isn't needed, so the body sheds it. That's a period!
basics.fact3: The menstrual cycle is about 21-35 days long
basics.fact4: It's a sign of a healthy, functioning body
basics.fact5: About half the world's population experiences periods
basics.biologyText: The menstrual cycle is controlled by hormones. These are natural chemicals in the body that send messages. Think of them like the body's text messages telling different parts what to do!

whyMiss.title: Why Girls Might Miss School or Feel Unwell
whyMiss.intro: Understanding why someone might not feel their best during their period helps you be more supportive.
whyMiss.crampsDesc: Muscle contractions in the uterus can cause stomach pain, similar to a muscle cramp during exercise
whyMiss.tirednessDesc: Hormonal changes and losing blood can make someone feel more tired than usual
whyMiss.headachesDesc: Changes in hormone levels can trigger headaches or make someone feel dizzy
whyMiss.moodChangesDesc: Hormones affect emotions, so someone might feel more sensitive, irritable, or sad
whyMiss.backPainDesc: The cramping can extend to the lower back, making it uncomfortable to sit or stand
whyMiss.understandingText: These symptoms aren't an excuse or exaggeration. They're real physical experiences. Some people have mild symptoms, others have severe ones. Being understanding and not making jokes makes a huge difference.

support.title: How to Be a Supportive Friend
support.intro: You can make a real difference by being understanding and helpful. Here's how:
support.do1Desc: If a friend seems tired or uncomfortable, give them space without prying
support.do2Desc: Don't make a big deal out of it. It's a regular part of life for many people
support.do3Desc: If someone needs a sweater or asks you to carry something, help out without questions
support.do4Desc: If a school club or sports team asks you to keep supplies, say yes
support.do5Desc: If you hear someone making period jokes, let them know it's not okay
support.dont1Desc: Period jokes aren't funny. They make people feel embarrassed and ashamed
support.dont2Desc: Don't ask someone if they're on their period. It's private
support.dont3Desc: It's natural biology, like sweating or growing. Don't act disgusted
support.dont4Desc: If someone has an accident, keep it private. Don't tell others
support.scenario1: A classmate seems quieter than usual
support.scenario1Action: Give them space, but let them know you're there if they need anything
support.scenario2: Someone asks to borrow your jacket
support.scenario2Action: Lend it without asking why. They might need it for privacy
support.scenario3: A friend says they can't play sports today
support.scenario3Action: Accept it without pressing for details. Suggest something low-key instead

myths.title: Busting Common Myths
myths.intro: There are many myths about periods that simply aren't true. Let's clear them up!
myths.fact1: Periods are completely natural and healthy. Menstrual blood is just blood and tissue, no different from a nosebleed
myths.myth2: Girls can't swim or exercise during periods
myths.fact2: Most people can do everything they normally do, including swimming, running, and playing sports. Exercise often helps reduce cramps!
myths.myth3: You can tell when someone has their period
myths.fact3: You cannot tell by looking at someone. Period products are designed to be discreet
myths.fact4: Most periods last 3-7 days. The average is about 5 days
myths.myth5: Only girls need to learn about periods
myths.fact5: Everyone benefits from understanding menstruation. It helps build supportive, educated communities
myths.fact6: Periods are a normal part of life. Open conversations help remove shame and stigma
myths.fact7: Period cramps are real and can be quite painful. They're caused by muscle contractions in the uterus
myths.myth8: You lose a lot of blood during a period
myths.fact8: The average period involves only about 2-3 tablespoons of blood. It might look like more because it's mixed with other fluids

girls.title: For Girls
girls.subtitle: Your Body, Your Journey
girls.intro: Your body is amazing! Let's learn about the changes happening and how to take care of yourself.
girls.whatToExpectContent: Periods usually start between ages 9-16. Everyone's body is different, and that's perfectly normal!
girls.yourCycleContent: A menstrual cycle is typically 21-35 days. The period itself usually lasts 3-7 days.
girls.takingCareContent: Learn about different period products, managing cramps, and when to talk to a doctor.
girls.feelingGoodContent: Tips for staying comfortable, eating well, and managing your emotions during your period.

faq.title: Frequently Asked Questions
faq.subtitle: Got questions? We've got answers!

questions.a1: A period is the monthly shedding of the uterine lining. It's a normal part of the menstrual cycle and usually lasts 3-7 days.
questions.q2: At what age do periods start?
questions.a2: Periods typically start between ages 9-16, with most girls getting their first period around 12-13 years old. Everyone's body is different!
questions.q3: Is it normal to have irregular periods?
questions.a3: Yes! Especially in the first few years. It can take 2-3 years for your cycle to become regular.
questions.a4: There are many options including pads, tampons, menstrual cups, and period underwear. You can choose what feels most comfortable for you.
questions.q5: Why do I feel emotional during my period?
questions.a5: Hormonal changes during your cycle can affect your mood. It's completely normal to feel more emotional. Self-care and rest can help!
questions.q6: Can I exercise during my period?
questions.a6: Absolutely! Exercise can actually help reduce cramps and improve your mood. Listen to your body and do what feels comfortable.
questions.a7: Mild to moderate cramping is normal. If pain is severe or interferes with daily activities, talk to a doctor or trusted adult.
questions.a8: Typically, people with female reproductive systems get periods. However, some transgender men may also experience periods.

parents.title: Guide for Parents
parents.subtitle: Supporting Your Child Through Puberty
parents.intro: As a parent, you play a crucial role in helping your child understand and navigate puberty.
parents.startConversationContent: Begin conversations early, before puberty starts. Use correct terminology and answer questions honestly.
parents.createSafeContent: Let your child know they can come to you with questions. Avoid showing embarrassment and normalize these discussions.
parents.resourcesContent: Books, websites, and healthcare providers can support your conversations.
parents.prepareKitContent: Help your daughter prepare a small kit with pads, clean underwear, and pain relief for school or activities.
